note.headline: Apple dips to 352.78, still above every value estimate as forecasts slip

summary.thesis: Apple is a strong, cash-rich grade-B business, but at 352.78 the price assumes much faster cash-flow growth than the business has delivered, while analysts keep lowering their forecasts.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait. Swing: wait, because the price sits between nearby support and a thin resistance zone with no clean setup.
summary.act_at: Long-term buy at 300.79 or lower; swing only on a close above 356.12

note.happening: Apple closed at 352.78, down 0.98% on the day, in a sideways range above its rising 20-, 50- and 200-day averages. News since the last note is product news only: reported smart-glasses progress, a reported test of daily usage limits for complex Siri AI requests, face unlock on the iPhone Duo, and Apple Watch Series 12 discounts before Black Friday. The next earnings report is on 2027-01-28, and analysts' forecasts slipped again over the past 30 days (-2.25%).
note.business: The business itself is in good shape. Trailing sales are 478.8B, up from 416.2B. Free cash flow (the cash left after running and investing in the business) is 136.1B, up from 98.8B. Operating margin rose to 33.01% from 31.97%, and the share count fell 1.56% in a year. Two things are at risk. First, growth is slowing: quarterly sales growth was 11.72%, down from 16.6% two quarters ago. Second, the latest filing shows inventory up 154% while quarterly sales rose 12%. Unsold products can force price cuts and squeeze margins. Analysts cut next-quarter EPS (earnings per share) by 3.8% over 30 days, so the slowdown is showing up in forecasts. The filing also adds a new risk related to an investigation. That is a governance and sentiment issue for now, with no number attached. Today's headlines (glasses, Siri limits, video podcasts, Mac security) are reports about products. None of them changes demand, margins or cash today. Apple also has more debt than cash (net cash -23.4B), but liquidity of 56.7B means its finances are not at risk.

worth.text: Every valuation method in DATA puts fair value below today's price. The cash-flow model (DCF, which values the company on the cash it may earn in future years) gives 144.23 in the bear case, 199.9 in the base case and 263.03 in the bull case. Apple's own price-to-sales history (price compared with sales per share) gives 222.27 to 300.79. To justify 352.78, the cash-flow model needs free cash flow to start growing at 27.4% a year. Last year's sales growth was 15%, and growth over three years was 8%. At a 20% starting growth rate the model gives 265.6. At 30% it gives 388.34. That growth rate is the single assumption behind the gap. The multiples point the same way. Apple trades at 39.3 times trailing earnings and 33.3 times next year's, and at 10.7 times sales against a peer median of 5.6. That price-to-sales level is the highest in its own 5-year history (100th percentile). My range is lower than last note's 226.4–321.32 because today's DCF values in DATA are lower.
worth.key_assumption: Starting free-cash-flow growth: the price needs 27.4%, while recent sales growth is 15% for last year and 8% a year over three years.
